questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compute an energy intensity from energy used and output delivered
questions.stem: The reef tank's return pump drew 3.1 kWh over four hours of filtration and moved 4.6 cubic metres of water in that time. Which statement correctly describes the energy intensity of that circulation?

options.text: The intensity is 0.22 kilowatt hours per cubic metre.
options.misconception: divides the hours into the energy instead.

options.text: The intensity is 1.48 cubic metres per kilowatt hour, because the volume should be divided by the energy.
options.misconception: inverts energy and volume and reports the ratio backwards

options.text: The intensity is 0.674 kilowatt hours per cubic metre, since 3.1 kWh over 4.6 cubic metres is the ratio.
The intensity is 3.1 kilowatt hours, because a pump's energy use is the meaningful measure on its own.
options.misconception: treats total energy as an intensity without normalising

questions.explanation: Energy intensity normalises energy used by output delivered, so 3.1 kWh over 4.6 cubic metres is 0.674 kWh per cubic metre. The four hours matter only because they set how much water passed.
questions.hint: Divide the energy by the volume of water moved.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a demand shift is not an energy saving
questions.learningObjective: Explain why shifting demand changes cost rather than energy
questions.stem: The facility moved the sump pump's run time from the afternoon tariff peak to the night tariff window, and the report claims a 22 percent energy saving. Explain what actually changed and why the saving claim does not follow.

answer.exemplar: Moving the pump to the night window changes when the electricity is used, not how much is used. The pump draws the same power for the same hours, so the total energy is unchanged and only the tariff applied to it differs. The saving is therefore on the bill rather than in the energy consumed, and it should be reported as a cost saving with the tariff periods stated rather than as a reduction in energy use.

questions.explanation: A demand shift moves the same energy to a different time, so total consumption and power draw are unchanged. What improves is the price paid per unit of energy.
questions.hint: The equipment ran for the same hours, so what changed?

About 4 percent of the standby unit's 5.5 kW rating is drawn while it waits.
options.misconception: divides by the standby unit rather than the installed total

options.text: About 50 percent of the installed capacity is idle, because one of the two pumps never runs.
options.misconception: counts the whole standby pump as wasted installed capacity

options.text: No capacity is idle, because a standby pump is required for reliability however small its load.
options.misconception: treats the presence of a standby unit.

questions.explanation: The running pump draws 5.5 kW and the standby unit trickles 0.22 kW, so the idle draw is 0.22 of the 11 kW installed, about 2 percent. A standby unit is needed for reliability.
questions.hint: Compare the standby draw with the total installed power.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of module temperature on array output

stimulus.body: Photovoltaic module log on the research station roof: 1.35 kW of rated output, module temperature 47 degrees Celsius at noon, ambient 22 degrees Celsius, and 4.9 kWh generated between 09:00 and 15:00 on a clear August day.

questions.stem: The roof module log records a hot summer midday. How does the elevated module temperature affect the day's output, and what would the same array produce at a lower temperature?

options.text: The module ran at about 45.6 kW, because the 47 degree reading exceeds the 1.35 kW rating by that factor.
options.misconception: divides a temperature by a power rating.

options.text: The array produced 4.9 kWh regardless of temperature, because cell voltage depends only on irradiance.
options.misconception: ignores the temperature effect on cell voltage

options.text: Output was reduced by the elevated cell temperature.
The elevated temperature means the 4.9 kWh figure is a metering fault and should be discarded.
options.misconception: treats a temperature effect as evidence of faulty metering

questions.explanation: Cell voltage falls as a module warms above its rated test temperature, so a hot module gives less power for the same irradiance and a cooler one would give more.
questions.hint: Cells lose voltage as they get warmer.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design an audit of a reported energy saving
questions.stem: A facility claims it has cut pumping energy by 18 percent since replacing the old circulation pumps. Describe how you would audit that claim and what you would need to establish.

answer.exemplar: Check whether the same water volume and the same operating hours were involved in both periods, because a fall in energy caused by running the pumps less is not a pump efficiency gain. Read the meters on the same circuits and compare the energy per cubic metre moved, and confirm that the replacement equipment was actually the one running. Establish whether any of the change came from a revised operating schedule or a change in tank stock rather than from the hardware, and report the adjusted saving with the adjustment stated.

questions.explanation: An audit must hold the service delivered constant, because the same savings appear if the tank is circulated less. The comparison is energy per cubic metre moved over the same hours.
questions.hint: Hold the service delivered constant.

options.misconception: objects to the time unit rather than the conditions

options.text: The comparison is not sound because the new lighting meter was read on a different meter class.
options.misconception: invents a meter specification that the record never mentions

The comparison is not sound because 31 kWh is too small a saving to be worth reporting.

questions.topic: Lifecycle boundaries in a payback comparison
questions.learningObjective: Explain why matching boundaries is required for a fair comparison
questions.stem: When comparing a heat pump with a resistance heater on energy payback, which statement best captures why the boundary matters?

options.text: The boundary only matters if the two options are bought on the same day from the same supplier.
options.misconception: reduces the boundary question to purchasing convenience

options.text: The boundary decides which energy flows are counted, so both options must be assessed over the same stages.
The boundary is set by the tax treatment of the capital spend and has no physical meaning.
options.misconception: treats an accounting choice as the whole story

options.text: The boundary only affects the payback figure if the equipment is replaced within the study period.
options.misconception: limits the importance of boundaries to one specific case

questions.explanation: A lifecycle boundary decides which energy flows count, such as manufacturing, transport, operation or end of life. Two options compared over different boundaries always give different answers.
questions.hint: What does the boundary actually select?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reverse cycle unit should be described
questions.stem: The tank's reverse cycle chiller cools the water and then warms the room with the recovered heat. Explain how the unit's energy performance should be described and why a single efficiency number can mislead.

answer.exemplar: The right way to describe a reverse cycle chiller is a coefficient of performance for cooling, which is heat removed from the water divided by electricity used, and a separate coefficient of performance for the heat returned to the room. Because the recovered heat is a real output, a single efficiency figure that ignores it makes the unit look far worse than it is, while adding both outputs together can make it look better than it is unless the boundary is stated clearly.

questions.explanation: A reverse cycle unit has two useful outputs, heat removed and heat returned to the room, so a single efficiency figure must state which outputs it includes.
questions.hint: There are two useful outputs here, not one.

options.text: About 2.7 kilowatt hours per square metre a day, because a year has 365 days that must be accounted for.
options.misconception: mixes a daily basis with the annual figure

options.text: About 29.4 kilowatt hours per square metre a month, because monthly reporting is the standard basis.
options.misconception: changes the reporting period without converting the total

questions.explanation: Building energy intensity divides annual energy by floor area, so 486,000 kWh over 620 square metres is about 784 kWh per square metre a year. It covers electricity only.
questions.hint: Annual energy divided by floor area.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of temperature losses in an array
questions.stem: I want to find out how much the elevated temperature of the roof modules is costing the research station in lost output. Describe the method and what you would report.

answer.exemplar: Log the module temperature with a surface sensor and the irradiance reaching the array, at short intervals through a representative month, and record the power output at the same time so each reading can be checked against the expected output at that irradiance and cell temperature. Compare the measured power with the nameplate output scaled for the measured irradiance and temperature, using the manufacturer's temperature coefficient. Report the monthly energy difference between the two, and note the hours when shading or soiling also affected the reading.

questions.explanation: The temperature effect is isolated by comparing measured output with what the same irradiance would give at the rated cell temperature. Soiling must be screened out in the same records.
questions.hint: Compare with the output expected when the cells are cool.

options.text: It has no operational emissions but still has emissions from manufacture, transport and end of life.

questions.topic: Standby and duty in a pump house
questions.learningObjective: Separate support loads from useful work in a duty cycle assessment
questions.stem: The pump house runs a duty pump, a standby pump and a blower around the clock. Explain how the duty cycle should be assessed so that standby losses are not confused with efficiency.

answer.exemplar: Start by separating the energy that actually moves water from the energy that keeps the system ready. The duty pump's draw over its running hours is useful work, while the standby pump's control and heating draw and the continuous blower are support loads that must be counted and then reduced rather than ignored. Assess the system by energy per cubic metre pumped and by the standby fraction of the total, and set targets on both, since a duty pump can be made more efficient while the standby load quietly grows.

questions.explanation: Support loads are real energy and must be separated from the work of moving water, or a duty pump looks more efficient than it is. The standby fraction of the total matters.
questions.hint: Not every kWh in the house moves water.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of delivered and recovered heat
questions.stem: I need to know how much heat the aquarium's reverse cycle unit actually delivers and how much heat it returns to the room. Describe the measurement method and the figures you would report.

answer.exemplar: Log the electricity drawn by the unit and use calibrated flow and temperature sensors on both the chilled water leaving the unit and the condensate side, so the heat removed from the tank can be calculated as mass flow times specific heat times temperature change. Measure the condensate temperature and flow to obtain the heat returned to the room, and take readings at the same intervals through a full day so part load behaviour is captured. Report the cooling coefficient of performance and the heating coefficient of performance separately, with the measurement boundary stated.

questions.explanation: Delivered heat must be measured from the water side, since the electricity meter cannot reveal how much heat was moved or returned to the room. Flow and temperature give the heat rate.
questions.hint: Measure flow and temperature on both sides of the unit.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why an intensity is more useful than an annual total
questions.stem: The facility's filtration plant moved 640,000 cubic metres of seawater last year using 218,000 kWh. Explain how this intensity should be reported and why it is more useful than the total.

answer.exemplar: The energy intensity of the plant is the electricity divided by the volume treated, so 218,000 kWh over 640,000 cubic metres is 0.341 kWh per cubic metre. Expressed that way the figure can be compared with other years, with other plants and with the performance each pump achieved separately. A total of 218,000 kWh on its own cannot be judged, because it says nothing about how much water was produced or whether the flow or the treatment requirement had changed.

questions.explanation: An intensity of 0.341 kWh per cubic metre lets the year be compared with others and with each pump's contribution, which a total cannot do. A total says nothing about the output.
questions.hint: Normalise the energy by the volume treated.

options.misconception: confuses the electricity purchased with the heat removed

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Standby and duty in a pump house
questions.learningObjective: Design a reduction in standby energy without losing reliability
questions.stem: I want to reduce the standby energy in the pump house without losing the reliability the standby pump provides. Describe a method and the results you would record.

answer.exemplar: Log the standby unit's draw continuously for a week to establish the real standby load rather than the nameplate figure, and break it into the control electronics, the anti-condensation heater and any valve or seal heating that is running unnecessarily. Then test each component separately by switching it off while watching the pump's readiness and the equipment's temperature, so the reliability requirement can be checked at the same time. Record the load removed and the effect on standby readiness for each change, and set a maximum standby power that the panel is then checked against.

questions.explanation: The standby load must be measured and split into its parts, because heating and controls often exceed the pump's own idle draw. Switching something off without checking readiness trades reliability.
questions.hint: Break the standby load into its components first.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: State what an audit of a reported saving must establish
questions.stem: A filtration upgrade is claimed to have saved 24 percent of the facility's pumping energy. Explain what an audit of that claim would need to establish and why.

answer.exemplar: The audit has to confirm that the same water was moved through the same filters over comparable hours, because treating fewer litres or fewer hours produces an identical apparent saving without any improvement in the equipment. The energy has to come from the same meter boundaries, since a new meter could have been installed at the same time as the upgrade. It also needs to check for changed operating rules, such as a new backwash schedule or a different filter setting, and any of those has to be subtracted before the residual is credited to the pumps.

questions.explanation: Any change in the service delivered, the meter boundaries or the operating rules shows up as an apparent saving and must be identified and removed.
questions.hint: Hold service, meters and operating rules constant.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Lifecycle boundaries in a payback comparison
questions.learningObjective: Set a lifecycle boundary and run a payback comparison
questions.stem: I need to compare a heat pump with a resistance heater for the tank room using energy payback. Describe how you would set the boundaries and carry out the comparison.

answer.exemplar: Define one boundary for both options and write down every energy flow inside it, such as manufacture, transport, installation, the electricity consumed during use and the disposal at end of life. Use the same boundary for the heater and the pump so neither option benefits from a different set of stages. Collect the energy figures for each stage from supplier data and from the metered electricity over the same operating hours, then divide the total embodied energy of each option by the annual energy it saves to get the payback in years, and state the boundary alongside the result.

questions.explanation: A comparison is meaningful only if both options are assessed over the same stages, and the boundary must be written down before the numbers are gathered and every flow quantified.
questions.hint: Write the boundary down before collecting any numbers.

options.text: Because the cell's voltage falls as it warms, so the same irradiance produces less power.
Because the module's power rating was measured on a cold day by mistake and is therefore wrong.

questions.topic: Standby and duty in a pump house
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a small continuous load can dominate a duty cycle
questions.stem: The pump house's weekly bill is dominated by the duty pump, which runs 14 hours a day, and by a blower that runs continuously at only 0.4 kW. Explain why the blower can still matter and what should be measured.

answer.exemplar: The blower's small power is misleading because it never stops, so over a week it accumulates 0.4 kW for 168 hours, which is 67 kWh, while the duty pump's figure is the product of a much larger power and a shorter time. A blower running continuously on a tank that only needs aeration for a few hours a day is a common form of waste. The measurement to make is the run hours from the timer or the control log against the tank's actual oxygen demand, and then a duty cycle that matches the requirement.

questions.explanation: A small power running for a long time can rival a large power running briefly, so weekly totals rather than nameplate powers decide what matters. The blower uses 67 kWh a week.
questions.hint: Power times hours decides the weekly energy.

options.misconception: mixes a partial cross-check with the full period balance

questions.explanation: The condenser releases the heat removed plus the electricity put in, so the heat removed is 118,400 minus 46,800, which is 71,600 kWh.
questions.hint: The condenser gives back heat removed plus work done.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of temperature loss in an array
questions.stem: I want to measure how much the temperature of the array's modules costs the station in lost output over a summer. Describe the method and the result you would report.

answer.exemplar: Fit a surface temperature sensor to a representative module and a pyranometer or reference cell alongside the array, and log both with the string's power output at short intervals through a clear month. Use the manufacturer's temperature coefficient to calculate the power the array would have produced at the rated cell temperature for the same irradiance, then compare with the measured output. Report the monthly energy difference and the percentage of output lost to temperature, and separate the loss from any soiling or shading effect found in the same records.

questions.explanation: The loss has to be calculated, using the temperature coefficient to work out what the same irradiance would have produced when cool. Soiling must be screened out.
questions.hint: Compare with the same irradiance on a cool module.

options.text: Lighting dominates the site, because 61,000 kWh is a large share of a 279,000 kWh total.

options.text: The two duties cannot be compared, because one treats seawater and the other treats the laboratory.

questions.explanation: Filtration's intensity is 218,000 kWh over 640,000 cubic metres, about 0.34 kWh per cubic metre. Lighting has no volume output, so it needs a different measure.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage energy reduction shown by metering
questions.stem: A pump was replaced and the report claims a saving of 2,700 kWh a quarter. The metered quarter before the change used 12,000 kWh and the quarter after used 9,000 kWh. What percentage reduction in energy use does the meter show?
questions.explanation: The reduction is 3,000 kWh over 12,000 kWh, exactly 25 percent. The claimed 2,700 kWh saving does not match the metered difference and must be explained before the improvement is accepted.

questions.topic: Standby and duty in a pump house

options.text: The figure is wrong because the standby pump's own idle draw was left out of the standby total from the start.
options.misconception: invents a missing component in the original measurement

options.text: The figure is wrong because a heater replacement cannot reduce standby losses at all in a pump house.

options.text: The 50 percent applies to the heater alone.
The figure is wrong because the new heater needs more watts in cold weather than in mild weather.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why delivered heat is reported separately from purchased energy
questions.stem: Why is it useful to state delivered heat separately from purchased energy when describing the tank room?

options.misconception: assumes delivered heat and purchased energy always coincide

options.text: Because the difference between them is the part of the purchase that did not become useful heat.
Because purchased energy includes the tariff charges that delivered heat excludes.
options.misconception: confuses the boundary of a measurement with the components.

options.text: Because delivered heat can be negative in some months and therefore needs a second figure.
options.misconception: invents a case where the delivered figure is negative

questions.explanation: Purchased energy is what the meter records and delivered heat is what reached the tank or room. The gap covers compressor and pump losses and any purchase that never became useful heat.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Lifecycle boundaries in a payback comparison
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an embodied-only comparison is incomplete
questions.stem: A new tank circulation pump and an older unit are being compared on embodied energy alone, with the new pump judged better because it uses less energy in service. Explain why that comparison is incomplete.

answer.exemplar: Judging on embodied energy alone ignores the energy the equipment consumes while it works, which for a pump is usually the larger part of its life cycle impact over many years of running. The two pumps also have different service lives, so the comparison has to state the years over which each is assumed to deliver the service. A fair comparison therefore needs one boundary that contains both the embodied stage and the operating stage, and it needs the service life of each unit stated so the results can be put on a common period.

questions.explanation: Embodied energy covers only making and delivery, so a smaller embodied stage does not make the new pump better overall. Operating energy and service life must sit inside the same boundary.
questions.hint: Which stage is missing from the comparison?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a demand shift is not an energy saving
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a cost saving from an energy saving in a schedule change

stimulus.body: Station metering note: chiller and lighting ran 6.0 hours a day on the old schedule at 12.4 kW average, and 6.0 hours a day on the new schedule at the same average power of 12.4 kW. The new schedule sits entirely inside the off-peak tariff window, which is priced at 0.09 units per kilowatt hour against 0.21 on the old window.

questions.stem: The metering note below sets out the old and new schedules and the two tariff prices. What did the schedule change achieve, and how should it be reported?

options.text: It achieved a 64 percent reduction in energy use, because the off-peak window consumes less power.
options.misconception: confuses a lower price with lower consumption

options.text: It left energy use unchanged and cut the electricity cost by about 64 percent.
It achieved a 64 percent reduction in energy use and a matching reduction in emissions.
options.misconception: assumes a price change also cuts the emissions

options.text: It achieved nothing, because a change of schedule cannot affect either the energy or the cost.
options.misconception: denies that the price paid for the same energy has changed

questions.explanation: The same 12.4 kW for 6.0 hours uses 74.4 kWh a day either way, so energy is unchanged. The cost falls from 74.4 times 0.21 to 74.4 times 0.09, about 64 percent less.
questions.hint: Compare the daily kilowatt hours, then the daily cost.
